## 1. What was read

**991 research articles** from 33 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **186** records (16% of the 1,177 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

| General | Cancer | Immune | Bioinfo | Sysbio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 391 | 176 | 74 | 518 | 18 |

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: bioinfo +91%, sysbio -25%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). Every journal on the roster contributed this month. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: Nucleic Acids Res 250, Bioinformatics 174, Nature 99, Science 77, JAMA 77, J Clin Oncol 61.

## 3. The evidence that moved it

!!! note "Written in arrears, and re-read from abstracts"
    2023 was added to the corpus after 2024, 2025 and 2026 had already been read,
    which is the opposite of the position the monthly practice is supposed to
    simulate. That has not changed and still caps what these months can support.
    What has changed is the reading. This month was first carded from titles and
    journal names alone, then re-scanned in full from abstracts on 2026-09-04
    with the instrument 2026 was read with. 2023 went from 25.1 to 80.4 cards per
    thousand research papers, against 2026's 84.8; 40% of this month's cards
    state something no title carries. The earlier version of this note said the
    thin record was a floor under the threads. It was a property of the
    instrument, and roughly three cards in four here were invisible to it.

**Plasma sequencing reads out resistance three times in one journal in one
month.** [36007218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36007218/) (*JCO*) resolves the acquired-resistance landscape to
anti-EGFR therapy in metastatic colorectal cancer; [36067452](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36067452/) does the same on
the cetuximab arm of CALGB/SWOG-80405; [36351210](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36351210/) reports that the mechanisms
differ by regimen and by line of therapy. Three independent groups, one target,
one month is the strongest evidence grade literature-only surveillance can
produce, and what they converge on is ctDNA answering *what next* rather than
*how bad*. [36646802](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36646802/) (*Nat Med*) ties molecular residual disease to whether
adjuvant chemotherapy works at all in colorectal cancer.

**Engineered cells reach patients in two compartments the platform is not built
for.** [36259971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36259971/) (*Cancer Discov*) delivers a B7-H3 CAR intraventricularly
into diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma and reports bioactivity; [36624315](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36624315/)
(*Nat Med*) takes an HLA-restricted TCR against a cancer-testis antigen through a
phase 1 across solid histologies. Both are small and single-arm, and neither is an
efficacy claim. What they establish is that the delivery route and the
manufacturing exist off the B-cell surface.

**Both non-lymphoid arms of the neuro-immune-microbiome thread run at top tier in
the same month.** [36517594](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36517594/) (*Nature*) reports glioma networks with autonomous
rhythmic electrical activity driving their own growth — neural excitability as a
tumour-intrinsic growth variable rather than as context. [36563680](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36563680/)
(*Cancer Cell*) puts gut bacterial nucleotide synthesis on the causal path of
neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy failure in rectal cancer. The thread's claim is that
these are one mechanism network and not three adjacent fields; this month they are
at least at one publication tier.

**A premalignant state with a mechanism attached.** [36656933](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36656933/) (*Science*): a
BTG1 mutation makes B cells supercompetitive and primes them for transformation.
[36098678](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36098678/) (*Cancer Discov*) reports cell competition shaping metastatic
latency and relapse in the same month. `interception` needs states that are
measurable *and* mechanistically distinct from cancer, and clonal competition is
the form both of these take.

**Foundation models open on a resource and two failures.** The only support is a
resource announcement — [36420884](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36420884/) (*NAR*), the RCSB PDB now serving a million
machine-computed structures alongside solved ones. Model output entering the
reference layer that everything downstream reads is a real change in the
substrate, and it is not a result. The two findings the month does carry both run
against the models: [36355460](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36355460/)
(*Bioinformatics*) optimises multiple sequence alignments end-to-end against
AlphaFold's own confidence and gets self-inconsistent, adversarial inputs, so the
confidence score can be gamed; [36692561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36692561/)
(*JAMA*) finds machine learning adds nothing over the pooled cohort equations for
stroke risk and performs worse in Black individuals. `foundation-models` opens
+1 / −2: a resource on the supporting side, and results only where the models
fail.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-09-04"
    This paragraph said the month's entire signal on the thread was the PDB
    resource plus news coverage of a chatbot, and that nothing in the 1,177
    titles read this month was a foundation-model finding. Two of them are, and
    the 2026-09-04 abstract re-scan carded both. Neither title states its verdict
    — one reads as a method paper, the other as an accuracy comparison — which is
    how a title-only pass came to read the month as empty rather than as adverse.
    The reading to withdraw is "thin", not the point about the resource.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

Three of this month's cards invert a population the field is organised around
removing, which is why `suppressive-population-inversion` opens at +0 / −4 — the
fourth card being [36577929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36577929/) (*Nat
Immunol*), where deleting PD-1 destabilises the lineage identity of
tumour-infiltrating regulatory T cells rather than only releasing the CD8
compartment. `next-gen-checkpoints` opens +1 / −3 on much of the same material;
its single support is [36585453](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36585453/) (*Nat
Cancer*), where blocking 4-1BB, LAG-3 and CXCR1/2 together produces durable
responses in pancreatic cancer that PD-1 blockade alone does not.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-09-04"
    This sentence said both threads open at zero support. `next-gen-checkpoints`
    opens +1 / −3: the abstract re-scan carded a combination-blockade result that
    a title-only pass had not collected. `suppressive-population-inversion` does
    open with no support, on four refutations rather than the three described
    below.

[36652534](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36652534/) (*Sci Transl Med*): CD200-positive cytotoxic T lymphocytes are
required for anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy to work. CD200 is an inhibitory ligand and its
axis is a standing checkpoint nomination; here the cells carrying it are the
effector, so blocking it removes what the therapy needs.

[36525971](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36525971/) (*Cancer Cell*): IL-5-producing CD4 T cells and eosinophils
cooperate to improve checkpoint response in breast cancer. Type 2 immunity is
routinely nominated as tumour-promoting; this is that nomination running the other
way, in a randomisable direction.

[36574773](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36574773/) (*Immunity*): CD39, the adenosine-axis ectonucleotidase pursued as
a blockade target, identifies the tumour-reactive CD8 compartment and predicts
checkpoint response in human lung cancer. In the same month [36040496](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36040496/) (*Blood*)
reports CD39/CD73 dysregulation driving T-cell immunosuppression in Sézary
syndrome. The molecule is being read as an effector marker and as a suppressive
effector at once, and this is only the opening half of that disagreement.

Three further results strain their threads from inside. [36638191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36638191/)
(*Sci Immunol*) shows that whether an anti-PD-1 antibody antagonises or agonises
the receptor is set by which epitope it binds — a variable a target-picking
programme does not control. [36646856](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36646856/) (*Nat Cancer*) locates checkpoint
resistance in an interferon-associated epigenetic memory the cancer cell carries
itself, which is the tumour-intrinsic explanation `immunotherapy-resistance`
claims the field is moving away from. And [36070539](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36070539/) (*JCO*) is the month's
cancer vaccine with an efficacy readout: a universal shared-antigen peptide
vaccine in refractory NSCLC, running on exactly the antigen space the neoantigen
claim says is insufficient.

The one card pushing the other way is [36563676](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36563676/) (*Immunity*), which puts
checkpoint resistance in the humoral compartment: the therapy itself alters IgG
glycosylation and the sialylated antibody blunts type I interferon.

### (b) Method credibility

Nine cards this month. The three described here escalate through different
objects, and none of those three is a model.

[36522432](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36522432/) (*Nat Genet*): guide RNAs validated against the reference genome
behave differently in different people, so a therapeutic editor's off-target
profile does not transfer from the reference to the patient. A reagent failing at
the level the clinic will meet it.

[36635510](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36635510/) (*Nature*): scientists cannot reliably distinguish
machine-generated abstracts from real ones. What is being audited is the readable
surface of the literature — the thing every downstream curation step, this corpus
included, treats as ground truth. [36653617](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36653617/) and [36624237](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36624237/) run beside it.

[36625810](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36625810/) (*JAMA*): devices cleared by claiming equivalence to earlier
devices that had themselves been recalled are more likely to be recalled in turn,
with [36625811](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36625811/) on which submission characteristics predict it. The object
here is neither a model nor an assay but the regulatory chain that certifies
instruments.

`method-credibility` reads −9 and will keep reading negative. Its `denominator`
field in `threads.yml` says why: the thread is a ledger of things found
unreliable, so the sign is very nearly fixed before any reading happens — 93% of
its cards across the whole corpus refute — and the ratio carries almost no
information. Read the volume and the object, never the sign.
